titleStmt.title: Letter from Donald Brace to Margaret West, March 31st 1936: A machine-readable transcription
titleStmt.author: Donald Brace

bibl.title: Letter from Donald Brace to Margaret West, March 31st 1936

projectDesc.p: Prepared by students of the 2026-2027 "The Book in the Digital Age: Agents and Medium" course, Book and Digital Media Studies, Leiden University

editorialDecl.p: I decided to stay as close as possible to the original analogue form of the letter I was assigned to transcribe. I have kept the line breaks and the line-end hyphen as they were. I also added a few short annotations and regularisations that I thought would be useful for the context of the letter. Moreover, I have appropriately tagged all of the people and organisations mentioned.

div.p:
Donald Brace informs the Company will likely work from the corrected proofs instead of the ones sent in instalments without corrections. He notes that West had planned for the manuscript to be ready for the printer by mid-March, but the first proofs' arrival indicates the Press is ahead of schedule. He says that West had planned publication for mid-May, but the corrected proofs only arrive days before, and the Company's time of publication will be too close to summer. Brace notes the Company could delay publication to August, but he doesn't prefer the 3+ months interval between English and American publication. He asks West to ask the Woolfs and states simultaneous publication would be best. He asks West if the Press plans to use Vanessa Bell's wrapper, and if so, when it can be seen. He also asks for a newer photograph of Virginia Woolf.
Typescript letter signed by Brace.

dateline.placeName:
HARCOURT, BRACE AND COMPANY, INC.
PUBLISHERS383 MADISON AVENUE, NEW YORK

opener.salute:
Dear Miss West
Manager of Leonard and Virginia Woolf's Hogarth Press. She was recruited for the role in February 1933.:

div.p:
Many thanks for your letters regarding Mrs. Woolf's new book.
I am especially delighted that you are sending the proofs in installments
and without waiting for the corrections. The proofs will be useful in all
sorts of ways, though I expect we shall wait for a corrected set before
setting. It usually works out that no time is lost by waiting for corrected
proofs, and of course expense is saved. I am not going to be able to resist
reading the installments as they come in; I have just read the first twelve
galleys, and I am watching every mail for more.
Your letter of February tenth said that you hoped to have the
manuscript ready for the printer about the middle of March and to dispatch
us a corrected proof from which to set about the end of April. The arrival
of these first proofs seems to indicate that you are so far somewhat ahead
of this tentative schedule. You also said in your letter of February tenth
that you were hoping to publish the book about the middle of May. I don't
know what can be done about it, but according to this tentative plan, we
should be receiving the finally corrected proof only a few days before your
date of publication. Evidently we are going to have a difficult decision
to make. If we hurry up and publish as promptly as we can, we are going to
be very close to the beginning of summer, which is probably not the best
time to publish, and we shall have less time than I should like for useful
advance work. Alternatively, we could put off publication here until early
autumn, or at any rate until August; but I dislike having so long an inter-
val, three months or more, between English and American publication. A good
many readers will be unwilling to wait so long for this new book, and there
is no way to prevent a considerable importation of your edition. I'd be
glad if you would mention this problem to Mr. and Mrs. Woolf and if they
would give such consideration to it as they can. The ideal, of course,
would be simultaneous publication. And any extent to which you feel able
to wait for us to catch up would be helpful.
Will you let me know whether you plan to use a wrapper by Vanessa Bell
British painter and interior designer.? If no, how soon may we see proof of it?
The most recent photograph we have of Mrs. Woolf has been used with FLUSHFlush: A Biography and THE WAVES
The Waves was published in 1931 and Flush: A Biography in 1933. So, there had not been a new photo of Virginia Woolf in 5 years at the time when the letter was written.. A never one would be valuable for us.

note.p: American publisher. His full name was Donald Clifford Brace. He was one of the founders of the New York publishing house Harcourt, Brace & Company.
